tldr: An offline reinforcement learning framework that pinpoints which action caused a failure in robot trajectories and redirects it toward successful actions from similar contexts, autonomously learning recovery behaviors without additional real-world trials.
hero_caption: Comparison between conventional methods and RedFlow. (a) Preference-based methods (such as DPO) evaluate only which full trajectory is better, leaving specific correction targets unclear. In contrast, (b) RedFlow identifies the actions responsible for failure and directly redirects them toward successful actions as targets.
overview:
Flow-matching VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models have attracted significant attention for their ability to express dexterous robot manipulation in a multimodal fashion. However, policies trained via imitation learning suffer from a fundamental weakness: when exposed to real-world conditions that deviate even slightly from training data, errors compound like a snowball, leading to unrecoverable failures.

While online reinforcement learning can acquire corrective behaviors, having a real robot undergo thousands of trial-and-error runs is impractical due to hardware wear and safety concerns. On the other hand, offline reinforcement learning from logged data either purely imitates successful trajectories or, like DPO, provides only coarse trajectory-level signals to avoid failure. Neither can instruct the robot at the action level on exactly how to recover.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed "RedFlow," a framework that turns collected failure data into action-level corrective signals. By clustering a compact representation combining estimated task progress from a pre-trained reward model and the robot's own joint states (proprioception), RedFlow redirects failed action chunks toward successful chunks executed in similar contexts.

Evaluated across all four suites of the LIBERO simulation benchmark and three real-world dual-arm robot manipulation tasks, RedFlow significantly outperformed existing offline RL baselines, boosting the real-robot success rate from 56.7% to 74.7%. Furthermore, it achieved performance on par with strong online RL methods like PPO while requiring roughly an order of magnitude less data.
contributions: Proposed Context-Aware Corrective Matching, which identifies locally failure-inducing actions within robot rollouts and assigns successful alternative actions without human intervention.

Designed the Adaptive Redirection Objective, unifying three distinct roles into a single loss: reinforcing high-quality actions, suppressing low-quality actions, and redirecting correctable actions toward targets.
Demonstrated significant improvements over existing offline RL baselines like AWR and DPO in both simulation (LIBERO) and three real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks.
Showed that task success rates comparable to online reinforcement learning methods (PPO, GRPO, DDPO) can be achieved with roughly an order of magnitude higher sample efficiency.

sections.heading: Don't Discard Failures! Turning Them into Action-Level Corrections
sections.summary: Imitation learning-based VLA models are vulnerable to compounding errors, making real-world failures inevitable. Because existing offline RL methods either discard failures or treat them at a coarse trajectory level, this work introduces RedFlow to convert failures into action-level corrective signals.
sections.details:
Flow-matching VLA policies are powerful because they model complex continuous actions by learning a velocity field that transports noise to action trajectories. However, simply imitating human demonstrations leaves them vulnerable to distribution shift during real-world deployment. Slight prediction errors compound over time, ultimately leading to fatal failures.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to address this issue, but repeated online trial-and-error on physical hardware does not scale due to hardware wear and human supervision costs. Conversely, offline RL learns safely from prior logs, yet conventional methods face a critical trade-off. Algorithms like AWR prioritize successful rollouts and discard failure logs entirely, while preference-based methods like DPO evaluate entire trajectories as bad without providing concrete guidance on which specific actions to fix and how.

Two main obstacles stand in the way:
- Granularity mismatch: Even failed trajectories often contain actions that were executed perfectly up to a certain point. Pinpointing exactly which step triggered the failure is challenging.
- Principled integration of corrective signals: Because flow matching uniformly imitates given data, carelessly feeding mixed-quality data into training can degrade performance instead of improving it.

RedFlow tackles these challenges through Context-Aware Corrective Matching, which retrieves successful actions in similar situations as corrective targets, and an Adaptive Redirection Objective, which pushes failures toward the target direction within the velocity field.

sections.heading: The Trend in Robot Learning: From Coarse Evaluation to Fine-Grained Action Correction
sections.summary: This section surveys offline post-training for VLAs and learning from process feedback. Unlike conventional evaluative rewards or preference learning, RedFlow uniquely derives direct continuous action-level corrective targets in a fully offline setting.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into two research streams.

The first is improving flow-matching VLA policies. While diffusion- and flow-matching-based action heads have recently driven progress in generalized robot manipulation, most remain confined to imitation learning. Although RL-based post-training has been explored, online RL entails prohibitive interaction costs, and standard offline RL tends to either focus solely on reinforcing successes or bluntly penalizing failures, failing to explicitly indicate what the robot should do instead.

The second stream is learning from failure using process feedback. Prior work has evaluated trajectory progress using reward models or leveraged human-in-the-loop (HIL) interventions. However, reward models alone only score whether a behavior is good or bad without generating concrete correction vectors. While human teleoperation interventions offer action-level guidance, they require dedicated human experts and lack scalability.

RedFlow's novelty lies in cleverly combining the robot's joint states with progress scores to extract constructive, action-level corrective signals purely from stored offline logs, without requiring any additional human intervention.

sections.heading: How RedFlow Works: Finding Success in Similar Contexts and Redirecting the Velocity Field
sections.summary: Execution contexts are defined using progress estimated by a pre-trained reward model alongside robot joint states, then clustered via HDBSCAN to determine correction targets. During training, flow matching is updated using a unified objective combining attraction to success, repulsion from failure, and redirection toward targets.
sections.details:
RedFlow's training pipeline consists of three main stages: action-level advantage estimation, context clustering for corrective target generation, and optimization via the adaptive redirection objective.

### 3.1 Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
The robot receives visual observations $I_t$ and proprioception $q_t$ as observation $o_t$, and outputs a continuous action chunk $a_t$ of length $K$ conditioned on language instruction $l$. The flow-matching policy $\pi_\theta$ generates the action $a_t = x_0$ by integrating the velocity field $v_\theta$ starting from noise $x_1$.

### 3.2 Context-Aware Corrective Matching
For each action chunk in the offline buffer, a surrogate $\hat{A}_t$ of the true action-level advantage is computed. Progress estimates $R(o_t, l)$ from a pre-trained Generalist Reward Model (GRM) are smoothed over a temporal window $W$, and local progress changes are combined with an episode-level outcome bias $b \cdot (2y_\tau - 1)$. Chunks with $\hat{A}_t > 0$ are classified as positive (successful), while those with $\hat{A}_t < 0$ are classified as negative (failed).

Next, to avoid clustering directly in high-dimensional image space, a compact feature space $f_t = [\tilde{q}_t, \beta \bar{p}_t]$ is constructed using normalized joint states $\tilde{q}_t$ and progress $\bar{p}_t$. HDBSCAN, a density-based clustering algorithm, is applied to this space. Chunks belonging to the same cluster are considered to be executing the same sub-task context. For a failed chunk $a_t$, a corrective target $a_t^*$ is obtained by computing the weighted centroid of successful chunks within that same cluster. Failed chunks that have no successful peers in their cluster or are labeled as outliers are treated as uncorrectable and undergo only failure suppression.

### 3.3 Adaptive Redirection Objective
The policy is updated using a composite loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}$ consisting of three terms:
- Quality-weighted attraction ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{att}}$): Strongly attracts high-quality actions weighted by a soft score $w_t$ derived from estimated quality.
- Failure suppression ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}$): A hinge loss that penalizes negative action chunks only when predicted actions fall within a margin $m$, pushing the policy away from failed actions.
- Target-guided correction ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cor}}$): For failed chunks with an assigned target $a_t^*$, this pulls the predicted action toward the target centroid.

Together, these components achieve a geometric transport that pushes probability mass out of failure regions bounded by a finite margin and redirects it toward verified nearby successful patterns.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Real-Robot Success Jumps to 74.7% with Emergent Recovery Behaviors
sections.summary: Evaluations across the LIBERO benchmark and three real-world dual-arm tasks showed RedFlow significantly outperforming baselines. It matched online RL performance with roughly 10x less data and demonstrated sophisticated emergent recoveries, such as retrieving slipped cloth using the opposite arm.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Simulation experiments were conducted on the LIBERO benchmark (40 tasks across Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites) using $\pi_0$ as the base policy. Real-robot experiments used an Agilex Cobot Magic dual-arm platform across three tasks: (a) cloth folding (bimanual coordination), (b) sweeping trash into a dustpan (tool manipulation), and (c) table cleaning (pick-and-place plus wiping).

### 4.2 Main Results (Simulation)
Compared to offline RL baselines AWR and DPO, RedFlow improved the average success rate across the four LIBERO suites from 56.2% (base policy) to 68.2% (+12.0 points). It substantially outperformed AWR (62.3%) and DPO (59.7%). The gain was especially notable on LIBERO-Goal, reaching 71.2% and outperforming DPO (51.8%) by nearly 20 points.

### 4.3 Ablation Study
Ablation experiments revealed key insights:
- Data composition: Removing failed rollouts dropped success to 68.0%, while removing successful rollouts dropped it to 62.4%, showing that both are essential to achieve 72.5%.
- Isolating uncorrectable failures: Forcing corrective targets onto failures without successful peers in their cluster degraded performance sharply to 61.0%, proving that erroneous correction targets are detrimental.
- Loss components: Removing the suppression term $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}$ yielded 68.8%, removing the correction term $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cor}}$ yielded 69.1%, and removing both dropped success to 65.7%, validating their synergistic effect.

### 4.4 Sample Efficiency Comparison
In comparisons with online RL methods (PPO, GRPO, DDPO), online approaches required approximately 13,000 to 16,000 fresh post-training rollouts to achieve a 75.8% success rate on LIBERO-Spatial. In contrast, RedFlow achieved the same threshold using only 1,536 fixed rollouts—roughly an order of magnitude fewer samples.

### 4.5 Real-Robot Experiments and Emergent Recovery
On the three physical robot tasks, RedFlow achieved an average success rate of 74.7% (compared to 56.7% for the base policy). In the challenging cloth folding task, success nearly doubled from 36.0% to 67.0% (+31.0 points).

Notably, the policy exhibited emergent recovery behaviors that were never explicitly demonstrated in the training data. For example, when the T-shirt slipped out of reach of the right arm during folding, the base policy repeatedly grasped empty air and failed. In contrast, the RedFlow-trained policy used its left arm to drag the shirt back within reach before resuming folding with both arms.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: RedFlow is a practical offline RL method that converts failure experiences of flow-matching VLA models into action-level corrective signals, demonstrating substantial improvements and remarkable sample efficiency across both simulation and real-world experiments.
sections.details:
This paper introduced RedFlow, a novel method that, instead of discarding deployment failures or coarsely penalizing them, retrieves successful examples from similar contexts to provide local corrective targets.

Experiments confirmed that RedFlow not only outperforms strong offline RL baselines and dramatically improves real-robot task success, but also matches online RL performance with roughly an order of magnitude fewer samples.

For future work, the authors highlight several directions: incorporating uncertainty-aware target assignment for out-of-distribution (OOD) states, scaling to longer-horizon tasks, and extending this offline formulation into an iterative online improvement loop.

sections.heading: Appendix: Theoretical Justification and Implementation Details
sections.summary: This section covers the theoretical interpretation of RedFlow's objective as local constrained optimal transport (Wasserstein gradient flows), along with rigorous hyperparameters and task definitions for simulation and real-robot evaluations.
sections.details:
The appendix provides theoretical interpretations of the methodology and detailed specifications for experimental reproducibility.

### Theoretical Interpretation (Appendix A)
The adaptive redirection objective is not merely a heuristic combination of loss terms; it can be formally interpreted as a single step of Constrained Wasserstein Policy Transport on the action distribution. Attraction to success, finite-margin suppression of failure, and redirection toward correction targets together construct a vector field that transports policy probability mass away from obstacle regions and toward safe, high-reward areas.

### Real-Robot Setup Details (Appendix D)
Physical experiments on the Agilex Cobot Magic utilize three camera views: two wrist cameras and one static front-view camera. Success criteria are strictly defined for each task: for sweeping, all 5 blocks must be swept into the dustpan, emptied into the trash bin, and the brush returned to the table; for table cleaning, 3 blocks must be stored into a bin and milk spills must be wiped clean with a cloth. Evaluations were conducted with 100 rollouts per condition, providing an exceptionally thorough and reliable sample size for physical robot experimentation.

takeaways: Rather than treating failure logs merely as negative examples to avoid, pairing them with successful actions from similar contexts turns them into direct action-level supervision for recovery.

Instead of clustering directly in high-dimensional image space, constructing a compact, semantically meaningful context space from robot proprioception and reward model progress scores is key in practice.
Differentiating uncorrectable failures—applying only suppression rather than forcing invalid correction targets—is essential for stable policy learning.
A well-designed pipeline for reusing offline failures can slash the sample requirements of hardware-intensive online reinforcement learning by an order of magnitude.
limitations: Assigning corrective targets heavily relies on the accuracy of GRM progress estimation and context clustering; noisy progress scores risk linking actions to incorrect targets.
For novel failures or extreme out-of-distribution (OOD) states that have no similar successful data in the buffer, corrective targets cannot be assigned, limiting the method to pure suppression.

Evaluations are restricted to a specific dual-arm platform and controlled environments; generalization under severe visual noise like dramatic lighting changes or over ultra-long-horizon tasks remains unverified.
